parts.latex: The time, $T$, in seconds that divers can hold their breath is normally distributed with $\mu=120$ and $\text{Var}(T)=400$. In what range of time length would you expect to find the middle 95%?

solutions.latex:
Since $\text{Var}(T)=\sigma^2=400$, $\sigma=20$.

The middle 95% lies within $2\sigma$ of the mean:
$$\begin{aligned} 120-2\times20&=80 \\ 120+2\times 20&=160 \end{aligned}$$
so $80\le x\le160$.

Hence the answer is (B).

parts.latex: The exact value of $I=\int_1^2 \dfrac{\ln x}{x}\,dx=\dfrac{1}{2}(\ln 2)^2$. The approximation of $I$ using the Trapezoidal Rule with 2 function values is

solutions.latex:
With 2 function values, $h=1$, so the trapezoidal rule gives
$$\begin{aligned} I&\approx\dfrac h2(\text{first value}+\text{last value}) \\ &=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac{\ln1}{1}+\dfrac{\ln2}{2}\right) \\ &=\dfrac14\ln2 \\ &\approx0.17328 \end{aligned}$$
The exact value is $\dfrac12(\ln2)^2\approx0.2402265$, so the approximation is smaller.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Percentage difference}&=\dfrac{\frac12(\ln2)^2-\frac14\ln2}{\frac12(\ln2)^2}\times100 \\ &\approx27.865\% \\ &\approx 28\% \end{aligned}$$
Hence the approximation is smaller by 28%, so the answer is (A).

parts.latex:
Given a function $f(x)=\dfrac{x}{x^2-5}$

Which of the following statements is true?

solutions.latex:
Test for even or odd:
$$\begin{aligned} f(-x)&=\dfrac{-x}{(-x)^2-5} \\ &=\dfrac{-x}{x^2-5} \\ &=-f(x) \end{aligned}$$
so $f$ is odd.

The graph has vertical asymptotes at $x=\pm\sqrt5$, and a horizontal line cuts it more than once (horizontal line test), so $f$ is many-to-one.

Hence the answer is (D).

parts.latex:
The amount $M$ of certain medicine present in the blood after $t$ hours is given by $M=9t^2-t^3$ for $0\le t\le 9$.

When is the amount of medicine in the blood increasing most rapidly?

solutions.latex:
The rate of increase of $M$ is
$$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=18t-3t^2=3t(6-t)$$
This is a concave-down parabola in $t$ with zeros at $t=0$ and $t=6$, so its maximum is at $t=3$.

Hence $M$ increases most rapidly at $t=3$, so the answer is (D).

parts.latex: $y=\sin^2 x$

solutions.latex:
Expand first:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=(4x-5)(4x+5) \\ &=16x^2-25 \end{aligned}$$
so
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=32x$$
Alternatively, by the product rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=4(4x+5)+(4x-5)\times4 \\ &=16x+20+16x-20 \\ &=32x \end{aligned}$$

Using the chain rule with $u=\sin x$, $y=u^2$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2\sin x\cos x$$
criteria: Correctly differentiates $\sin^2 x$ to get $2\sin x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: In an arithmetic series, the third term is 5 and the tenth term is 26. Find the sum of the first 14 terms.

solutions.latex:
The third and tenth terms give two equations:
$$\begin{aligned} a+2d&=5 \\ a+9d&=26 \end{aligned}$$
Subtracting gives $7d=21$, so $d=3$ and $a=-1$.

Using $S_n=\dfrac n2\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{14}&=\dfrac{14}{2}\big(2(-1)+13\times3\big) \\ &=259 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly finds $a$ and $d$, or applies the sum formula correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Evaluate

$$\int_1^4 5(9x-4)^4\,dx$$

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_1^45(9x-4)^4\,dx&=\left[5\times\dfrac{(9x-4)^5}{5\times9}\right]_1^4 \\ &=\dfrac19\left[(9x-4)^5\right]_1^4 \\ &=\dfrac19\left[(9(4)-4)^5-(9-4)^5\right] \\ &=\dfrac19\left[32^5-5^5\right] \\ &=3727923 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex:
Solve the following equation for $x$.

$$e^{2x}+3e^x-10=0.$$

solutions.latex:
Let $m=e^x$, so the equation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} m^2+3m-10&=0 \\ (m+5)(m-2)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
so $m=-5$ or $m=2$.

$e^x=-5$ has no solution, since $e^x>0$.

$e^x=2$ gives $x=\ln2$.
$$\therefore\ x=\ln 2$$
criteria: Correctly reduces to a quadratic equation and solves it, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2 x)=2\tan x\,\sec^2 x$.
Hence find $\int \tan x\,\sec^2 x\,dx$.

solutions.latex:
Write $\sec^2x=(\cos x)^{-2}$ and differentiate by the chain rule:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2x)&=\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cos x)^{-2} \\ &=-2\cos^{-3}x\cdot(-\sin x) \\ &=\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos^3x} \\ &=\dfrac{2\sin x}{\cos x}\times\dfrac{1}{\cos^2x} \\ &=2\tan x\sec^2x \end{aligned}$$
as required.

From part (i),
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sec^2x)=2\tan x\sec^2x$$
so, ignoring the constant,
$$\sec^2x=\int2\tan x\sec^2x\,dx$$
Hence
$$\int\tan x\sec^2x\,dx=\dfrac12\sec^2x+C$$
(equivalently $\dfrac12(1+\tan^2x)+C$).

parts.latex: Show that $f(x)$ represents probability density function.
Find the mode of the probability density function $f(x)$.

solutions.latex:
$f(x)$ is a probability density function if $f(x)\ge0$ on its domain and $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx=1$.

For $0\le x\le1$, $6x(1-x)\ge0$.
$$\begin{aligned} \displaystyle\int_0^1(6x-6x^2)\,dx&=\left[3x^2-2x^3\right]_0^1 \\ &=(3-2)-0 \\ &=1 \end{aligned}$$
Hence $f(x)$ is a probability density function.
criteria: Finds $\displaystyle\int f(x)\,dx$ correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The mode is where $f(x)$ is greatest.

Since $f(x)=6x(1-x)$ is a concave-down parabola with zeros at $0$ and $1$, its maximum lies midway between them.
$$\therefore\ \text{mode}=x=\dfrac12$$

parts.latex:
Find the value(s) of $b$ such that $y=2x+b$ is a tangent to the parabola

$$y=2x^2+6x-5.$$

solutions.latex:
The gradient of the tangent is $2$, so set the derivative equal to $2$:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=4x+6=2 \\ x&=-1 \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=2(-1)^2+6(-1)-5=-9$, so the point of contact is $(-1,-9)$.

Substituting into $y=2x+b$:
$$\begin{aligned} -9&=2(-1)+b \\ b&=-7 \end{aligned}$$
Alternatively, equate the two equations:
$$2x+b=2x^2+6x-5$$
so $2x^2+4x-5-b=0$. A tangent means one solution, so $\Delta=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=4^2-4(2)(-5-b) \\ &=16+40+8b \end{aligned}$$
so $b=-7$.
$$\therefore\ b=-7$$
criteria: Finds the point of contact using calculus, or forms the quadratic by solving simultaneously and attempts $\Delta=0$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source noted the guidelines write the constant as $m$ while the paper uses $b$; $b$ used here.

5013.stem: Angela guesses three questions in her multiple choice test, which has four options per question. Find the probability that Angela gets:

parts.latex: Only one correct answer.
At least one correct answer.

solutions.latex:
Let $C$ be a correct answer and $IC$ an incorrect answer, with $P(C)=\dfrac{1}{4}$ and $P(IC)=\dfrac{3}{4}$. There are three orders for exactly one correct answer.
$$\begin{aligned} P&=P(C\,IC\,IC)+P(IC\,C\,IC)+P(IC\,IC\,C) \\ &=3\times\dfrac{1}{4}\times\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^2 \\ &=\dfrac{27}{64} \end{aligned}$$

Use the complement: at least one correct is the opposite of none correct.
$$\begin{aligned} P(\text{at least one correct})&=1-P(\text{no correct}) \\ &=1-\left(\dfrac{3}{4}\right)^3 \\ &=\dfrac{37}{64} \end{aligned}$$

5017.stem:
A surveyor stands at a point $P$, which is due east of the tower $OT$, of height $h$ metres. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower $T$ from $P$ is $30^\circ$. The surveyor then walks 100 metres to point $B$, which is on a bearing of $150^\circ$ from the foot of tower $O$. The angle of elevation of the top of the tower from $B$ is now $45^\circ$.

\exfigure{1270_q13b_1}

figures.cap: tower OT with P east of O, B on bearing 150 from O, BP = 100 m, elevations 45 degrees at B and 30 degrees at P

parts.latex: Express the length of $OP$ in terms of $h$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, whole question removed

parts.latex: Show that $(100)^2=h^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^2 30^\circ}-\dfrac{h^2}{\tan 30^\circ}$.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, whole question removed

parts.latex: Hence find the height of the tower. Answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.note: 3D trigonometry (tower seen from two points): now Year 11 Extension 1, whole question removed

solutions.latex:
In $\triangle OPT$, the angle at $O$ is a right angle, so
$$\begin{aligned} \tan30^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{OP} \\ OP&=\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ} \\ &=\sqrt{3}\,h \end{aligned}$$

$P$ is due east of $O$ and $B$ is on a bearing of $150^\circ$ from $O$, so $\angle BOP=150^\circ-90^\circ=60^\circ$.

In $\triangle BOT$:
$$\begin{aligned} \tan45^\circ&=\dfrac{h}{BO} \\ BO&=h \end{aligned}$$
Apply the cosine rule in $\triangle OPB$:
$$\begin{aligned} BP^2&=BO^2+OP^2-2\cdot BO\cdot OP\cos\angle BOP \\ 100^2&=h^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^230^\circ}-2h\times\dfrac{h}{\tan30^\circ}\times\dfrac{1}{2} \\ &=h^2+\dfrac{h^2}{\tan^230^\circ}-\dfrac{h^2}{\tan30^\circ} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $OB$ and applies the cosine rule in $\triangle OPB$ correctly, or finds $OB$ and $\angle BOP=60^\circ$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Factorise $h^2$.
$$100^2=h^2\left(1+\dfrac{1}{\tan^230^\circ}-\dfrac{1}{\tan30^\circ}\right)$$
So
$$\begin{aligned} h^2&=\dfrac{100^2}{1+\frac{1}{\tan^230^\circ}-\frac{1}{\tan30^\circ}} \\ &=4409.269852\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ h\approx 66.4 \text{ m (1 d.p.)}$$

parts.latex: Find the domain of $f(x)$.
Find any stationary point(s) and determine their nature.
Find any point(s) of inflection.
Sketch the graph of $f(x)=\ln(x^2+1)$ showing all features from part (ii) and (iii).

solutions.latex:
The logarithm needs $x^2+1>0$, which is true for all real $x$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the domain is all real } x$$

$$f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$$
For stationary points, set $f'(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1} \\ x&=0 \end{aligned}$$
Then $y=\ln(0+1)=0$, so $(0,0)$ is a stationary point.

Nature, by the sign of $f'(x)$:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1&: f'(-1)=-1 &&\text{decreasing}\\ x=0&: f'(0)=0 &&\text{stationary}\\ x=1&: f'(1)=1 &&\text{increasing} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient goes $-,0,+$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.

Alternatively,
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{2-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
and $f''(0)=2>0$, so $(0,0)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the stationary point correctly, or determines its nature correctly, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the quotient rule on $f'(x)=\dfrac{2x}{x^2+1}$:
$$f''(x)=\dfrac{2(x^2+1)-2x(2x)}{(x^2+1)^2}=\dfrac{2-2x^2}{(x^2+1)^2}$$
Set $f''(x)=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-2x^2&=0 \\ x&=\pm1 \end{aligned}$$
Possible points of inflexion are $(1,\ln2)$ and $(-1,\ln2)$.

Test the concavity:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-2&: f''=-\dfrac{6}{25} &&\text{concave down}\\ x=-1&: f''=0 \\ x=0&: f''=2 &&\text{concave up}\\ x=1&: f''=0 \\ x=2&: f''=-\dfrac{6}{25} &&\text{concave down} \end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes at $x=\pm1$.

$$\therefore\ (1,\ln2)\text{ and }(-1,\ln2)\text{ are points of inflexion}$$

criteria: Correct shape, or shows the features from parts (ii) and (iii) correctly, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Prove the following identity

$$(1+\tan x)^2=2\tan x+\sec^2 x$$
Hence find the area bounded by $y=(1+\tan x)^2$ and the $x$-axis between $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$.

solutions.latex:
Use $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{LHS}&=(1+\tan x)^2 \\ &=1+2\tan x+\tan^2x \\ &=1+\tan^2x+2\tan x \\ &=\sec^2x+2\tan x \\ &=\text{RHS} \end{aligned}$$

Since $(1+\tan x)^2\ge0$ for $-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\le x\le\dfrac{\pi}{4}$, the area is the integral, using part (i).
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Area}&=\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(1+\tan x)^2\,dx \\ &=\displaystyle\int_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}}(2\tan x+\sec^2x)\,dx \\ &=\Big[-2\ln|\cos x|+\tan x\Big]_{-\frac{\pi}{4}}^{\frac{\pi}{4}} \\ &=\left(-2\ln\left|\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right|+1\right)-\left(-2\ln\left|\cos\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{4}\right)\right|+(-1)\right) \\ &=2 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly uses part (i) and integrates $\tan x$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: State the amplitude and period.
Find the exact values of all intercepts of $y=2\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ with the axes for $0\le x\le\pi$.
Hence sketch the graph of $y=2\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)$ for $0\le x\le\pi$, showing all features from part (i) and (ii) and the global maximum and minimum.

solutions.latex:
For $y=a\sin(bx-c)$, the amplitude is $|a|$ and the period is $\dfrac{2\pi}{b}$.
$$\text{Amplitude}=2$$
$$T=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$$
criteria: Correct amplitude or correct period, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
For the $y$-intercept, put $x=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= 2\sin\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) \\ &= -2\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ &= -\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
So the $y$-intercept is $(0,-\sqrt{3})$.

For the $x$-intercepts, put $y=0$.
$$\sin\left(2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)=0$$
So $2x-\dfrac{\pi}{3}=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi$, giving
$$x=\dfrac{\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6}$$
The last value is outside the domain $0\le x\le\pi$.

$$\therefore\ \text{the } x\text{-intercepts are } \left(\dfrac{\pi}{6},0\right) \text{ and } \left(\dfrac{2\pi}{3},0\right)$$

5022.stem:
A bag contains three red balls and four black balls. Two balls are selected at random without replacement from the bag.

Let $X$ be the number of black balls drawn.

parts.latex:
Fill in the following table and hence find exact value of $E(X)$.

\extable{1270_q14c_t1}
Find $E(X^2)$ and hence find $\text{Var}(X)$ and standard deviation $\sigma$.

solutions.latex:
Probabilities of the number of black balls drawn, without replacement:
$$\begin{aligned} P(0) &= \dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{2}{6}=\dfrac{1}{7} \\ P(1) &= 2\times\dfrac{3}{7}\times\dfrac{4}{6}=\dfrac{4}{7} \\ P(2) &= \dfrac{4}{7}\times\dfrac{3}{6}=\dfrac{2}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c} x & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ \hline P(X=x) & \dfrac{1}{7} & \dfrac{4}{7} & \dfrac{2}{7} \end{array}$$
$$\begin{aligned} E(X) &= \sum x\,p(x) \\ &= 0\times\dfrac{1}{7}+1\times\dfrac{4}{7}+2\times\dfrac{2}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{8}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds correct $E(X)=\mu$ from an incorrect table of values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2) &= \sum x^2p(x) \\ &= 0\times\dfrac{1}{7}+1^2\times\dfrac{4}{7}+2^2\times\dfrac{2}{7} \\ &= \dfrac{12}{7} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X) &= E(X^2)-\mu^2 \\ &= \dfrac{12}{7}-\left(\dfrac{8}{7}\right)^2 \\ &= \dfrac{20}{49} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \sigma &= \sqrt{\dfrac{20}{49}} \\ &= 0.638876\ldots \\ &\approx 0.639 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct $E(X^2)$, or finds $\text{Var}(X)$, or equivalent merit

5023.stem: The velocity $v$ of a particle in metres per second is given by the formula $v=5(1+e^{-t})$, where $t$ is the time in seconds.

figures.cap: solution sketch: marking guideline sketch of v=5(1+e^-t) with asymptote v=5

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity of the particle.
Is the particle ever stationary? Justify your answer.
Sketch the graph of the velocity.
Find the total distance travelled by the particle in the first 5 seconds.

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 5(1+e^0) \\ &= 10 \text{ m/s} \end{aligned}$$

The particle is stationary when $v=0$:
$$0=5(1+e^{-t})$$
This has no solution, since $e^{-t}>0$ makes $1+e^{-t}>1$.

$$\therefore\ v\ne 0,\text{ so the particle is never stationary.}$$

As $t\to\infty$, $v\to 5(1+0)=5$, so $v=5$ is a horizontal asymptote.

\exfigure{1270_q15a_s1}
criteria: Correct shape and $y$-intercept, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Since $v>0$ for all $t$, the distance equals the integral of $v$.
$$\begin{aligned} d &= \int_0^5 5(1+e^{-t})\,dt \\ &= 5\Big[t-e^{-t}\Big]_0^5 \\ &= 5\left[5-e^{-5}-(0-e^0)\right] \\ &= 5\left(5-e^{-5}+1\right) \\ &= 30-5e^{-5} \text{ metres} \end{aligned}$$
This is $29.97$ m (2 d.p.).

1270_q15a_s1.notes: v=5(1+e^{-t}) drawn from the equation with a dot at (0,10) and the dashed asymptote v=5 ending in an arrow. One true y-scale is a compromise between the crop's 10 and 5 positions; the sketch is not to scale, with 10 drawn higher. Dropped the teacher's working 't→∞, v→5(1+0), v→5' (rule 17), which is most of the red. Curve 0.9pt, aux dashes, filled arrowheads.

5024.stem: The line $y=mx$ is a tangent to the curve $y=\ln(2x-1)$ at a point $P$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: marking guideline sketch of y=mx tangent to y=ln(2x-1) at P

parts.latex: Sketch the line and the curve on the same diagram, clearly indicating the point $P$.
Show that the coordinates of $P$ are $\left(\dfrac{2+m}{2m},\dfrac{2+m}{2}\right)$.
Hence show that $2+m=\ln\left(\dfrac{4}{m^2}\right)$.

solutions.latex:
The curve $y=\ln(2x-1)$ needs $2x-1>0$, so $x>\dfrac{1}{2}$.

When $y=0$, $2x-1=1$, so $x=1$ is the $x$-intercept.

The line $y=mx$ passes through $(0,0)$.

\exfigure{1270_q15b_s1}
criteria: Correct log graph, or correct line through $(0,0)$ with the point of contact $P$ clearly indicated, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $y=\ln(2x-1)$:
$$y'=\dfrac{2}{2x-1}$$
The line $y=mx$ is tangent at $P$, so the gradient there is $m$:
$$m=\dfrac{2}{2x-1}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2x-1 &= \dfrac{2}{m} \\ 2x &= \dfrac{2}{m}+1 \\ x_P &= \dfrac{1}{m}+\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{2+m}{2m} \end{aligned}$$
Substituting into $y=mx$:
$$\begin{aligned} y_P &= m\times\dfrac{2+m}{2m} \\ &= \dfrac{2+m}{2} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P\left(\dfrac{2+m}{2m},\dfrac{2+m}{2}\right)$$
criteria: Equates $y'=m$ and solves for $x$, or substitutes the $x$-value into one of the equations, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The point $P\left(\dfrac{2+m}{2m},\dfrac{2+m}{2}\right)$ from part (ii) lies on $y=\ln(2x-1)$, so its coordinates satisfy the equation.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{2+m}{2} &= \ln\left(2\left(\dfrac{2+m}{2m}\right)-1\right) \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2+m}{m}-1\right) \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{m}+\dfrac{m}{m}-1\right) \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{m}\right) \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} 2+m &= 2\ln\left(\dfrac{2}{m}\right) \\ &= \ln\left(\dfrac{2}{m}\right)^2 \\ &= \ln\dfrac{4}{m^2} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Substitutes coordinates of $P$ into $y=\ln(2x-1)$ and attempts to solve it, or equivalent merit

1270_q15b_s1.notes: y=ln(2x-1) and its true tangent from the origin: m≈0.5575 solves 2+m=ln(4/m^2), so P=(2.294,1.279) is at its computed position (rules 12, 16). The x-scale matches the crop's 1 and the asymptote x=1/2. The y-scale (75 px/unit) was picked so the line's slope and P match the crop. Kept the dashed asymptote, dots at P and (1,0), and the labels O, 1, P(x,y), y=mx, y=ln(2x-1). The lower branch follows the true log, so it reaches the asymptote slightly further left than the hand sketch. Light grey grid. Low original-coverage score is almost all scanned grid paper.

5025.stem:
Given the probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}2e^{-2x} & x\ge 0\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distribution function $F(x)$.
Hence find the median.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x 2e^{-2x}\,dx \\ &= 2\times\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\Big[e^{-2x}\Big]_0^x \\ &= -\left[e^{-2x}-e^0\right] \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=1-e^{-2x}\quad (x\ge 0)$$

Let $m$ be the median, so $F(m)=\dfrac{1}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2} &= 1-e^{-2m} \\ e^{-2m} &= \dfrac{1}{2} \\ -2m &= \ln\dfrac{1}{2} \\ m &= -\dfrac{1}{2}\ln\dfrac{1}{2}=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2\ (=\ln\sqrt{2}\approx 0.347)$$
criteria: Equates $F(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}$ and shows significant progress to find the value of the median, or equivalent merit

5026.stem:
Michelle borrows \$450 000 to be repaid by regular monthly repayments of \$$M$ over a period of 25 years at 6% per annum reducible monthly. Interest is calculated and charged just before each repayment.

Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$-repayments.

parts.latex:
Show that the expression for the amount owing after two repayments is

$$A_2=450\,000(1.005)^2-M(1.005)-M.$$

Show that the amount owing after $n$-repayments is

$$A_n=450\,000(1.005)^n-M\,\dfrac{(1.005)^n-1}{0.005}.$$
Calculate the amount of each regular monthly repayment.

solutions.latex:
After one repayment, interest is $\dfrac{6}{12}=0.5\%$ per month.
$$A_1=450000(1.005)-M$$
The next month, interest is charged on $A_1$, then $M$ is repaid.
$$\begin{aligned} A_2 &= A_1(1.005)-M \\ &= 450000(1.005)^2-M(1.005)-M \end{aligned}$$
as required.

meta.format_note: Source noted that the guidelines write the repayment as $P$; the paper uses $M$, and $M$ is used here.

solutions.latex:
Following the pattern from part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 450000(1.005)^n-M(1.005)^{n-1}-\cdots-M \\ &= 450000(1.005)^n-M\left(1.005^{n-1}+\cdots+1\right) \end{aligned}$$
The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms, with sum $\dfrac{r^n-1}{r-1}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A_n &= 450000(1.005)^n-M\,\dfrac{(1.005)^n-1}{1.005-1} \\ &= 450000(1.005)^n-M\,\dfrac{(1.005)^n-1}{0.005} \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Correctly applies the pattern from (i), or correctly applies the sum of a GP formula, or equivalent merit
Using part (ii), correctly equates $A_{300}=0$ and attempts to solve it for the repayment, or equivalent merit

5027.stem:
An isosceles triangle $\triangle ABC$ is inscribed within a unit circle centred at $O$, as shown in the diagram below. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$, $\angle BAC=\theta$ and $\angle BOM=\theta$.

\exfigure{1270_q16b_1}

figures.cap: isosceles triangle ABC inscribed in a unit circle, centre O, M midpoint of BC

parts.latex: Show that the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $A=\sin\theta\,(1+\cos\theta)$.
Hence prove that the area of the isosceles triangle $\triangle ABC$ is maximum when it is equilateral.

solutions.latex:
Take $BC$ as the base and $AM$ as the height ($AM\perp BC$).
$$\text{Area}=\dfrac{1}{2}\times BC\times AM$$
In right-angled $\triangle OBM$ (with $OB=1$): $BM=\sin\theta$ and $OM=\cos\theta$.

So $AM=AO+OM=1+\cos\theta$ and $BC=2BM=2\sin\theta$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{2}\times 2\sin\theta\times(1+\cos\theta) \\ &= \sin\theta(1+\cos\theta) \end{aligned}$$
as required.
criteria: Finds $BC$ or $AM$ in terms of $\theta$, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule on $A=\sin\theta(1+\cos\theta)$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=\sin\theta & v&=1+\cos\theta\\ u'&=\cos\theta & v'&=-\sin\theta\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} A' &= \cos\theta(1+\cos\theta)-\sin^2\theta \\ &= \cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-\sin^2\theta \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points: $A'=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0 &= \cos\theta+\cos^2\theta-(1-\cos^2\theta) \\ &= 2\cos^2\theta+\cos\theta-1 \\ &= (2\cos\theta-1)(\cos\theta+1) \end{aligned}$$
So $\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ or $\cos\theta=-1$.

$\cos\theta=\dfrac{1}{2}$ gives $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ ($\dfrac{5\pi}{3}$ is impossible in a triangle).

$\cos\theta=-1$ gives $\theta=\pi$, which is impossible.

Hence $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ is the only solution.

Nature, testing the sign of $A'$:
$$\begin{aligned} \theta=1 &: A'=0.124 &&(>0) \\ \theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3} &: A'=0 \\ \theta=1.1 &: A'=-0.135 &&(<0) \end{aligned}$$
The gradient goes $+,0,-$, so $\theta=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$ is a maximum.

Since $\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $\angle BAC=\dfrac{\pi}{3}$, it is equilateral.

$$\therefore\ \text{the area is a maximum when the triangle is equilateral.}$$
criteria: Finds the stationary point correctly, or equivalent merit
Differentiates the area formula correctly and attempts to solve $A'=0$, or equivalent merit

Right-angle mark at M, single ticks on AB and AC, double ticks on BM and MC, labels A, B, C, M, O, θ, θ, 1, 1. The crop's solid black angle sectors are drawn as black!30 (rule 5, 'too overkill'). Lines are 0.6pt rather than the scan's heavy strokes (rule 3), which explains most of the red. The circle is about 5 px smaller than the scan's so that it passes exactly through the vertices.

figures.cap: graphs of y=f(x) above and y=g(x) below the x-axis, with vertical line x=2

parts.latex: Write down a definite integral that gives the value of $A$.
The function $f(x)$ from part (i) is given by $f(x)=x^2e^{kx}$, where $k$ is a positive constant. Show that $f'(x)=xe^{kx}(kx+2)$.
Using the results of part (i) and (ii), or otherwise, find the value of $k$ such that $A=\dfrac{16}{k}$.

solutions.latex:
The region lies between $f(x)$ (above) and $g(x)$ (below) from $x=0$ to $x=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^2\big(f(x)-g(x)\big)\,dx \\ &= \int_0^2\left[x^2e^{kx}-\left(-\dfrac{2xe^{kx}}{k}\right)\right]dx \end{aligned}$$

Using the product rule on $f(x)=x^2e^{kx}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x^2 & v&=e^{kx}\\ u'&=2x & v'&=ke^{kx}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} f'(x) &= 2xe^{kx}+x^2\cdot ke^{kx} \\ &= xe^{kx}(2+kx) \end{aligned}$$
as required.

From part (i):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \int_0^2\left[x^2e^{kx}+\dfrac{2xe^{kx}}{k}\right]dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{k}\int_0^2\left(kx^2e^{kx}+2xe^{kx}\right)dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{k}\int_0^2 xe^{kx}(kx+2)\,dx \end{aligned}$$
By part (ii), the integrand is $f'(x)$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \dfrac{1}{k}\int_0^2 f'(x)\,dx \\ &= \dfrac{1}{k}\Big[x^2e^{kx}\Big]_0^2 \end{aligned}$$
Put $A=\dfrac{16}{k}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{16}{k} &= \dfrac{1}{k}\Big[x^2e^{kx}\Big]_0^2 \\ 16 &= 2^2e^{2k}-0 \\ 4 &= e^{2k} \\ \ln 4 &= 2k \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ k=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 4=\ln 2$$
criteria: Simplifies the integral to $A=\dfrac{1}{k}\int_0^2 f'(x)\,dx$, or equivalent merit

Kept the dashed line x=2 (aux), the dot at (2,0), double-ended axes and the labels y=f(x), y=g(x), x=2, 2, 0, x, y. Curves 0.9pt since they touch the axis (rule 9). parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ ?

solutions.latex:
The graph of $f(x)=\sqrt{1-x^2}$ is a semicircle of radius $1$ centred at the origin.

The square root needs $1-x^2\ge 0$, so $-1\le x\le 1$.

$$\therefore\ \text{domain } [-1,1]$$

parts.latex: What is the angle of inclination of the line $\sqrt{3}x-y+2\sqrt{3}=0$ with respect to the positive $x$-axis?

solutions.latex:
Rearrange to gradient form.
$$\begin{aligned} \sqrt{3}x-y+2\sqrt{3}&=0 \\ y&=\sqrt{3}x+2\sqrt{3} \end{aligned}$$
The gradient equals $\tan\theta$, so $\tan\theta=\sqrt{3}$.
$$\therefore\ \theta=60^\circ$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equal to $\dfrac{\log_3 32}{\log_3 2}$ ?

solutions.latex:
Write $32=2^5$ and use the log power rule.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\log_3 32}{\log_3 2}&=\dfrac{\log_3 2^5}{\log_3 2} \\ &=\dfrac{5\log_3 2}{\log_3 2} \\ &=5 \end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex:
The time taken to travel between two regional cities is approximately normally distributed with a mean of 85 minutes and a standard deviation of 4 minutes.

The percentage of travel times that are between 81 minutes and 93 minutes is closest to

solutions.latex:
$81$ is $1$ standard deviation below the mean of $85$, and $93$ is $2$ standard deviations above it.

Between $-1$ and $+1$ sd is $68\%$; between $-2$ and $+2$ sd is $95\%$, so each of the extra bands $1$ to $2$ sd above the mean holds $\dfrac{95\%-68\%}{2}$.
$$68\%+\dfrac{95\%-68\%}{2}=81.5\%$$
Hence the answer is option C.

parts.latex:
A box contains five red marbles and four blue marbles. Stella selects three marbles at random, without replacing them.

The probability that at least one of the marbles that Stella selects is red is

solutions.latex:

5040.stem: In an arithmetic series, the first term is $18$ and the sum of the first $20$ terms is $1310$.

parts.latex: Show that the $20^{\text{th}}$ term is $113$.
Find the common difference.
Find the sum of first $35$ terms.

solutions.latex:
Using the sum formula $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}(a+l)$ with $a=18$, $n=20$:
$$\begin{aligned} 1310&=\dfrac{20}{2}(18+l) \\ 131&=18+l \\ l&=131-18 \\ &=113 \end{aligned}$$

Using $T_n=a+(n-1)d$ with $T_{20}=113$:
$$\begin{aligned} 113&=18+19d \\ 95&=19d \\ d&=5 \end{aligned}$$

Using $S_n=\dfrac{n}{2}\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$:
$$\begin{aligned} S_{35}&=\dfrac{35}{2}\big(2\times18+(35-1)\times5\big) \\ &=3605 \end{aligned}$$

Using the quotient rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{u}{v}\right)=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^{3x}-5 & v&=x+1 \\ u'&=3e^{3x} & v'&=1 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=\dfrac{(x+1)\times3e^{3x}-(e^{3x}-5)\times1}{(x+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{3xe^{3x}+3e^{3x}-e^{3x}+5}{(x+1)^2} \\ &=\dfrac{3xe^{3x}+2e^{3x}+5}{(x+1)^2} \end{aligned}$$

solutions.latex:
The series is geometric with $a=750$ and ratio:
$$r=-\dfrac{300}{750}=-\dfrac{2}{5}$$
Since $|r|<1$, the limiting sum exists.
$$\begin{aligned} S&=\dfrac{a}{1-r} \\ &=\dfrac{750}{1-\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right)} \\ &=\dfrac{3750}{7} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $r$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: The first four terms of a geometric sequence are $48, m, n$ and $750$. Find the values of $m$ and $n$.

solutions.latex:
The terms are $a, ar, ar^2, ar^3$, so
$$\begin{aligned} a&=48 &&(1)\\ ar&=m &&(2)\\ ar^2&=n &&(3)\\ ar^3&=750 &&(4)\end{aligned}$$
Substitute (1) into (4):
$$\begin{aligned} 48r^3&=750\\ r^3&=\dfrac{125}{8}\\ r&=\sqrt[3]{\dfrac{125}{8}}=\dfrac{5}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Then
$$\begin{aligned} m&=48\times\dfrac{5}{2}=120\\ n&=48\times\left(\dfrac{5}{2}\right)^2=300\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m=120,\ n=300$$
criteria: Finds the correct value of $r$, or equivalent merit

5054.stem: Consider the curve given by $y=3x-x^3-1$, for $-3\le x\le 2$.

figures.cap: solution sketch: sketch of y=3x-x^3-1 on -3<=x<=2 with labelled points (-3,17), (-1,-3), (0,-1), (1,1), (2,-3)

parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
Find the point of inflection.
Sketch the curve for $-3\le x\le 2$, showing all key features.
What is the maximum value of this function for $-3\le x\le 2$.

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} y&=3x-x^3-1\\ y'&=3-3x^2\\ y''&=-6x\end{aligned}$$
For stationary points, $y'=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3-3x^2&=0\\ x^2&=1\\ x&=\pm1\end{aligned}$$
At $x=1$:
$$y=3-1-1=1,\qquad y''=-6<0$$
$\therefore\ (1,1)$ is a maximum turning point.

At $x=-1$:
$$y=-3+1-1=-3,\qquad y''=6>0$$
$\therefore\ (-1,-3)$ is a minimum turning point.
criteria: Finds the coordinates of all the stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds the correct values of $x$ for the stationary points, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Possible inflection where $y''=0$:
$$\begin{aligned} -6x&=0\\ x&=0\end{aligned}$$
Then $y=-1$.

Test the concavity either side:
$$\begin{aligned} x=-1:&\ y''=6>0 &&\text{concave up}\\ x=1:&\ y''=-6<0 &&\text{concave down}\end{aligned}$$
The concavity changes, so $(0,-1)$ is a point of inflection.

criteria: Correct sketch showing some key features, or equivalent merit

$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum value of } y \text{ is } 17 \text{ for } -3\le x\le 2$$

5055.stem: The chocolate consumption per person per day of a population of people was found to be normally distributed with a mean of $68.95$ grams and a standard deviation of $18.45$.

parts.latex: Above what chocolate consumption rate does $2.5\%$ of this population lie?
Rahul consumed $50.5$ grams of chocolate in one day. What percentage of this population have a chocolate consumption rate more than Rahul’s?

If Ben takes a sample of people from this population and finds that $6$ of them consumed less than $13.6$ grams of chocolate per person per day. If Ben’s sample has the same distribution as this population, what is Ben’s sample size?

solutions.latex:
$2.5\%$ of the population lies above $2$ standard deviations from the mean ($z=2$).
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 68.95+2\times18.45 \\ &= 105.85 \text{ grams} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 2.5\% \text{ of this population consumed more than } 105.85 \text{ grams of chocolate per person per day.}$$

Find the $z$-score of Rahul's consumption.
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{50.5-68.95}{18.45} \\ &= -1 \end{aligned}$$
The proportion within $1$ standard deviation of the mean is $68\%$, so the proportion below $z=-1$ is
$$\dfrac12(100\%-68\%)=16\%$$
The proportion above is
$$100\%-16\%=84\%$$
$$\therefore\ 84\% \text{ of people consumed more than } 50.5 \text{ grams of chocolate per person per day.}$$

Find the $z$-score of $13.6$ grams.
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{13.6-68.95}{18.45} \\ &= -3 \end{aligned}$$
The proportion within $3$ standard deviations of the mean is $99.7\%$, so the proportion below $z=-3$ is
$$\dfrac12(100\%-99.7\%)=0.15\%$$
This $0.15\%$ of the sample represents $6$ people, so
$$\dfrac{6}{0.15\%}=4000$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the sample size is } 4000 \text{ people.}$$

5056.stem:
The length of time, in minutes, that a customer queues to buy toilet paper is a random variable, $X$, with probability density function

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}k(64-x^2) & \text{for } 0\le x\le 8\\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

where $k$ is a constant.

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is $\dfrac{3}{1024}$.
Find the cumulative distribution function.
Find the probability that a customer will queue for longer than $5$ minutes, round your answer to $4$ significant figures.
can_use: Probabilities from a probability density function

solutions.latex:
The total probability is $1$, so
$$\int_0^8 k(64-x^2)\,dx=1$$
$$\begin{aligned} k\left[64x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^8 &= 1 \\ k\left[64\times8-\dfrac{8^3}{3}-0\right] &= 1 \\ k\times\dfrac{1024}{3} &= 1 \\ k &= \dfrac{3}{1024} \end{aligned}$$

The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$ for $0\le x\le 8$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x) &= \int_0^x \dfrac{3}{1024}(64-t^2)\,dt \\ &= \dfrac{3}{1024}\left[64t-\dfrac{t^3}{3}\right]_0^x \\ &= \dfrac{3}{1024}\left(64x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{3x}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{1024} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ F(x)=\begin{cases}0 & x<0\\[6pt] \dfrac{3x}{16}-\dfrac{x^3}{1024} & 0\le x\le8\\[6pt] 1 & x>8\end{cases}$$

meta.format_note: Source used $x$ as both the limit and the dummy variable; changed the dummy variable to $t$ (notation only).

solutions.latex:
$$\begin{aligned} P(X>5) &= 1-P(X\le5) \\ &= 1-F(5) \\ &= 1-\left(\dfrac{3}{16}\times5-\dfrac{5^3}{1024}\right) \\ &= \dfrac{189}{1024} \\ &= 0.184570\dots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ P(X>5)\approx0.1846 \text{ (4 significant figures)}$$

5057.stem:
The diagram below shows the graphs of $y=5-x$ and $y=\dfrac{4}{2x-1}$

\exfigure{1271_q29_1}

figures.cap: line y=5-x and hyperbola meeting at A and B with region between shaded

parts.latex: Show that the $x$-coordinate values of $A$ and $B$ are $1$ and $4.5$ respectively.
Find the exact area of the shaded region.

solutions.latex:
Method 1: substitute each $x$ value into both equations, where $y_1=5-x$ and $y_2=\dfrac{4}{2x-1}$.

When $x=1$:
$$y_1=5-1=4,\qquad y_2=\dfrac{4}{2\times1-1}=4$$
so $y_1=y_2$.

When $x=4.5$:
$$y_1=5-4.5=0.5,\qquad y_2=\dfrac{4}{2\times4.5-1}=0.5$$
so $y_1=y_2$.

Method 2: solve simultaneously.
$$\begin{aligned} 5-x &= \dfrac{4}{2x-1} \\ (5-x)(2x-1) &= 4 \\ 10x-5-2x^2+x &= 4 \\ -2x^2+11x-5-4 &= 0 \\ 2x^2-11x+9 &= 0 \\ (2x-9)(x-1) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=1 \text{ or } x=4.5$$

On $1\le x\le4.5$ the line lies above the curve, so the shaded area is
$$A=\int_1^{4.5}\left(5-x-\dfrac{4}{2x-1}\right)dx$$
$$\begin{aligned} A &= \left[5x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-2\ln|2x-1|\right]_1^{4.5} \\ &= \left(5\times4.5-\dfrac{4.5^2}{2}-2\ln|2\times4.5-1|\right)-\left(5\times1-\dfrac{1^2}{2}-2\ln|2\times1-1|\right) \\ &= \left(\dfrac{99}{8}-2\ln8\right)-\left(\dfrac92-2\ln1\right) \\ &= \dfrac{63}{8}-2\ln8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ A=\left(\dfrac{63}{8}-2\ln8\right)\text{ units}^2$$

5058.stem: A gardener plants a bed of roses. The bed is planted so that the first row has $24$ rose plants. The second row has $29$ rose plants. Each succeeding row has $5$ more rose plants than the previous row.

parts.latex: Calculate the number of rose plants in the $8^{\text{th}}$ row.
Which row would be the first to contain more than $150$ rose plants?
The gardener has planted $2895$ rose plants altogether. Assuming that the above pattern has been continued, how many rows were planted?

solutions.latex:
The sequence is an arithmetic progression with $a=24$ and $d=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} T_8 &= 24+(8-1)\times5 \\ &= 59 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 8^{\text{th}} \text{ row has } 59 \text{ rose plants.}$$

Find the first $n$ for which $T_n>150$.
$$\begin{aligned} 24+(n-1)\times5 &> 150 \\ 24+5n-5 &> 150 \\ 5n &> 131 \\ n &> \dfrac{131}{5} \\ n &> 26\dfrac15 \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ is a whole number, $n=27$.
$$\therefore\ \text{the } 27^{\text{th}} \text{ row is the first row to contain more than } 150 \text{ rose plants.}$$

The total number of plants is the sum of the first $n$ terms, $S_n=\dfrac n2\big(2a+(n-1)d\big)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2895 &= \dfrac n2\big(2\times24+(n-1)\times5\big) \\ 5790 &= n(48+5n-5) \\ 5790 &= 43n+5n^2 \\ 0 &= 5n^2+43n-5790 \\ 0 &= (n-30)(5n+193) \end{aligned}$$
So $n=30$ or $n=-\dfrac{193}{5}$. Since $n$ must be positive, $n=30$.
$$\therefore\ 30 \text{ rows were planted.}$$

5059.stem:
A particle moves in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds its displacement is $x$ metres from the origin $O$ on the line. The velocity of this particle is given by

$$v=2-4\cos 2t,\qquad 0\le t\le 2\pi$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: graph of v=2-4cos2t for 0<=t<=2pi

parts.latex: Find the initial velocity of this particle.
Find all the times when the particle is at rest, where $0\le t\le 2\pi$.
Sketch the graph of $v$ as a function in terms of $t$, showing all key features.
Find the acceleration of the particle when $t=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
Find the exact displacement of this particle when $t=\pi$ given that its initial displacement is $3$ metres to the right of the origin.

solutions.latex:
The initial velocity is the velocity at $t=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} v &= 2-4\cos0 \\ &= 2-4 \\ &= -2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the initial velocity is } -2 \text{ m/s.}$$

The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2-4\cos2t &= 0 \\ 4\cos2t &= 2 \\ \cos2t &= \dfrac12 \end{aligned}$$
Since $0\le t\le2\pi$, we need $0\le2t\le4\pi$.
$$2t=\dfrac\pi3,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{3}$$
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac\pi6,\ \dfrac{5\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{6},\ \dfrac{11\pi}{6}$$
\exfigure{1271_q31_s1}
criteria: Correct graph with some key features shown

solutions.latex:
Method 1: from the graph of $v$, at $t=\dfrac\pi2$ there is a maximum turning point of the velocity function, so the acceleration is $0 \text{ m/s}^2$.

Method 2: acceleration is the derivative of velocity.
$$\ddot x=\dfrac{dv}{dt}=8\sin2t$$
When $t=\dfrac\pi2$:
$$\ddot x=8\sin\pi=0$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the acceleration is } 0 \text{ m/s}^2$$

Displacement is the integral of velocity.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= \int(2-4\cos2t)\,dt \\ &= 2t-2\sin2t+C \end{aligned}$$
When $t=0$, $x=3$:
$$3=0-2\sin0+C,\quad\text{so } C=3$$
Hence $x=2t-2\sin2t+3$.

When $t=\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 2\pi-2\sin2\pi+3 \\ &= 2\pi+3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the displacement is } (2\pi+3) \text{ metres to the right of the origin when } t=\pi.$$

The curve crosses the axis at pi/6, 5pi/6, 7pi/6 and 11pi/6, so those four labels would touch it below or above the axis. figures.cap: window: rectangle of height h surmounted by semi-circle of radius r (not to scale)

parts.latex:
Given that the perimeter of the window is to be $16\pi$ metres, show that

$$h=8\pi-r-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r$$

Hence, show that the area $A$ of the window is given by the formula

$$A=16\pi r-2r^2-\dfrac{1}{2}\pi r^2$$
Find the exact radius of the semi-circle for which the area of the window is to be a maximum.
Find the maximum area of this window correct to 1 decimal place.

solutions.latex:
The perimeter is made up of two vertical sides, the base and the semicircular arc.
$$\text{Perimeter}=2h+2r+\pi r$$
Given that the perimeter is $16\pi$:
$$\begin{aligned} 16\pi &= 2h+2r+\pi r \\ 2h &= 16\pi-2r-\pi r \\ h &= 8\pi-r-\dfrac12\pi r \end{aligned}$$

The area is the rectangle (width $2r$, height $h$) plus the semicircle.
$$A=2rh+\dfrac12\pi r^2$$
Substitute $h=8\pi-r-\dfrac12\pi r$ from part (a):
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 2r\left(8\pi-r-\dfrac{\pi r}{2}\right)+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2} \\ &= 16\pi r-2r^2-\pi r^2+\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2} \\ &= 16\pi r-2r^2-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2} \end{aligned}$$

Differentiate the area with respect to $r$.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dr}=16\pi-4r-\pi r$$
Stationary point: $\dfrac{dA}{dr}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 16\pi-4r-\pi r &= 0 \\ 4r+\pi r &= 16\pi \\ r(4+\pi) &= 16\pi \\ r &= \dfrac{16\pi}{4+\pi} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dr^2}=-4-\pi<0$$
So the stationary point is a maximum.
$$\therefore\ r=\dfrac{16\pi}{4+\pi}\text{ metres gives the maximum area.}$$

Substitute $r=\dfrac{16\pi}{4+\pi}$ into $A=16\pi r-2r^2-\dfrac{\pi r^2}{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A &= 16\pi\times\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{4+\pi}\right)-2\times\left(\dfrac{16\pi}{4+\pi}\right)^2-\dfrac{\pi\times\left(\frac{16\pi}{4+\pi}\right)^2}{2} \\ &= 176.8946\dots \\ &\approx 176.9 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the maximum area of the window is } 176.9 \text{ m}^2$$

parts.latex: What is the value of $(\log a)^2\div\log\left(a^2\right)$ ?

solutions.latex:
Using the log law $\log\left(a^2\right)=2\log a$:
$$\begin{aligned}(\log a)^2\div\log\left(a^2\right)&=\dfrac{(\log a)^2}{2\log a}\\&=\dfrac{\log a}{2}\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Which of the following is equal to $\dfrac{4^n-1}{2^n-1}$ ?

solutions.latex:
Write $4^n=\left(2^n\right)^2$, then use the difference of two squares.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{4^n-1}{2^n-1}&=\dfrac{\left(2^n\right)^2-1^2}{2^n-1}\\&=\dfrac{\left(2^n-1\right)\left(2^n+1\right)}{2^n-1}\\&=2^n+1\end{aligned}$$
This matches option A.

parts.latex: For a normally distributed set of scores, which of the following statements is FALSE?

solutions.latex:
Option A claims $P(z>2)$ is higher than $P(z>1)$.

Further from the mean means a smaller tail area:
$$P(z>2)\approx 0.023,\qquad P(z>1)\approx 0.159$$
So $P(z>2)<P(z>1)$ and statement A is false.

The other statements are true for a normal distribution: it is symmetric about the mean, the $z$-score measures distance from the mean in standard deviations, and the mean equals the median.

The false statement is option A.

solutions.latex:
A vertical line meets the curve more than once, for example $x=2$ gives $y=-2,\ 0$ and $2$.

Check: substituting $x=2$ gives $4+4y-y^3=4$, so $y\left(4-y^2\right)=0$, giving $y=0,\ 2,\ -2$.

So one $x$ value has many $y$ values (one-to-many).

A horizontal line also meets the curve more than once, for example $y=0$ at $x=-2$ and $x=2$. So one $y$ value has many $x$ values (many-to-one).

Therefore the relation is many-to-many, which is option D.

The shaded area is the integral over the first quarter period:

So $\dfrac{a}{2}=1$ and $a=2$.

Now integrate over $\left[0,\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right]$:
$$\begin{aligned}\int_0^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}2\cos 2x\,dx&=\Big[\sin 2x\Big]_0^{\frac{3\pi}{4}}\\&=\sin\dfrac{3\pi}{2}-\sin 0\\&=-1\end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Find the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y=e^x\sin x$ as it passes through the origin.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=e^x & v&=\sin x\\ u'&=e^x & v'&=\cos x\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x\\ &=e^x(\cos x+\sin x)\end{aligned}$$
At $x=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}y'&=e^0(\cos 0+\sin 0)\\ &=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the gradient at the origin is } 1$$

parts.latex: Two ordinary 6-sided dice, one red and one blue, are rolled and the numbers on the uppermost face are recorded. The blue die shows a number less than five. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is greater than seven?

solutions.latex:
Given the blue die shows less than five, it is 1, 2, 3 or 4, each with probability $\dfrac{1}{4}$. For a sum greater than seven, the red die must show:

blue 2: red 6; blue 3: red 5 or 6; blue 4: red 4, 5 or 6 (blue 1 cannot work).
$$\begin{aligned}P(\text{sum}>7)&=\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{1}{6}+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{2}{6}+\dfrac{1}{4}\times\dfrac{3}{6}\\ &=\dfrac{1+2+3}{24}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Some progress towards the correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A set of scores is normally distributed. A score of 12 has $z$-score of $-2$ while a score of 21 has a $z$-score of $+1$.

Calculate the mean of the scores.

solutions.latex:
From $z=-2$ to $z=1$ is 3 standard deviations, and this spans $21-12=9$.
$$\sigma=\dfrac{9}{3}=3$$
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ with $x=12$, $z=-2$:
$$\begin{aligned}-2&=\dfrac{12-\mu}{3}\\ -6&=12-\mu\\ \mu&=18\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct calculation of the standard deviation, or other progress towards the answer

5078.stem: A cup of coffee is cooling according to the following exponential formula $C=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2t}\right)$, where $C$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius and $t$ is the time in minutes since the coffee was poured.

parts.latex: Calculate the initial temperature of the coffee.
Calculate the temperature of the coffee after 10 minutes, correct to the nearest degree.
After how many minutes, to the nearest minute, will the coffee first reach $50^\circ\text{C}$?

solutions.latex:
At $t=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}C&=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2\times 0}\right)\\ &=95^\circ\text{C}\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}C&=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2\times 10}\right)\\ &=21+\left(74\times 3^{-2}\right)\\ &=29.2222\ldots\\ &\approx 29^\circ\text{C (to the nearest degree)}\end{aligned}$$

$$\begin{aligned}50&=21+\left(74\times 3^{-0.2t}\right)\\ \dfrac{29}{74}&=3^{-0.2t}\\ \log_3\left(\dfrac{29}{74}\right)&=-0.2t\\ t&=-5\log_3\left(\dfrac{29}{74}\right)\end{aligned}$$
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned}t&=\dfrac{-5\ln\left(\frac{29}{74}\right)}{\ln 3}\\ &\approx 4\text{ minutes and 15 seconds}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ t\approx 4\text{ minutes (nearest minute)}$$
criteria: Progress towards the correct answer, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Show that $\dfrac{\sec\theta-\sec\theta\cos^4\theta}{1+\cos^2\theta}=\sin\theta\tan\theta$.

solutions.latex: $$\begin{aligned}\text{LHS}&=\dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^4\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{\sec\theta\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)}{1+\cos^2\theta}\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)\\ &=\dfrac{1}{\cos\theta}\times\sin^2\theta\\ &=\dfrac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\times\sin\theta\\ &=\sin\theta\tan\theta\\ &=\text{RHS}\end{aligned}$$

5085.stem: The displacement of a particle moving along the $x$-axis is given by $x=t+e^{-2t}$, where $x$ is the displacement from the origin in metres and $t$ is the time in seconds, for $t\ge 0$.

parts.latex: Find an expression, in terms of $t$, for the velocity of the particle.
Find the time when the particle is closest to the origin.

solutions.latex:
The velocity is the derivative of the displacement.
$$v=\dfrac{dx}{dt}=1-2e^{-2t}$$

The particle is closest to the origin at a minimum of $x$, which is possible where $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=1-2e^{-2t} \\ e^{-2t}&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ e^{2t}&=2 \\ 2t&=\ln 2 \\ t&=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \end{aligned}$$
The acceleration is $a=4e^{-2t}$, which is positive for all $t$.

Hence any turning point is a global minimum.
$$\therefore\ t=\dfrac{1}{2}\ln 2 \text{ seconds}$$
criteria: Finds the correct time, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the stationary points and determine their nature.
Given that the point $(1,-16)$ lies on the curve, show that it is a point of inflection.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=(x+1)^2 & v&=x-5\\ u'&=2(x+1) & v'&=1\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=2(x+1)(x-5)+(x+1)^2 \\ &=(x+1)(2x-10+x+1) \\ &=3(x+1)(x-3) \end{aligned}$$
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$, so $x=-1$ and $x=3$.

For the second derivative:
$$\begin{aligned} y'&=3(x^2-2x-3) \\ y''&=3(2x-2)=6(x-1) \end{aligned}$$
At $x=-1$, $y''=-12<0$, so a local maximum.

At $x=3$, $y''=12>0$, so a local minimum.

$y(-1)=0$ and $y(3)=4^2\times(-2)=-32$.
$$\therefore\ \text{local maximum at } (-1,0),\ \text{local minimum at } (3,-32)$$
criteria: Correctly determines one stationary point and its nature, or equivalent merit

5089.stem:
The time $t$ minutes that a customer spends waiting in a queue has a probability density function:

$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{x(k-x)}{36} & \text{for } 0\le x\le k\\[2mm] 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$

figures.cap: solution sketch: symmetric pdf curve on [0,6] with axis of symmetry at x = 3

parts.latex: Show that the value of $k$ is 6.
Write down the value of $E(X)$.
Calculate $\text{Var}(X)$.

solutions.latex:
The total probability is 1, so $\displaystyle\int_0^k f(x)\,dx=1$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{36}\int_0^k(kx-x^2)\,dx&=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{kx^2}{2}-\dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^k \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{k^3}{2}-\dfrac{k^3}{3}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{3k^3-2k^3}{6}\right] \\ &=\dfrac{k^3}{216} \end{aligned}$$
So $\dfrac{k^3}{216}=1$.
$$\therefore\ k=\sqrt[3]{216}=6$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards the solution

solutions.latex:
Use $\text{Var}(X)=E(X^2)-E(X)^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} E(X^2)&=\dfrac{1}{36}\int_0^6x^3(6-x)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\int_0^6(6x^3-x^4)\,dx \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[\dfrac{3x^4}{2}-\dfrac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^6 \\ &=\dfrac{1}{36}\left[1944-\dfrac{7776}{5}\right] \\ &=10.8 \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Var}(X)&=10.8-3^2 \\ &=1.8 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards the answer

parts.latex:
Chickens are sized according to their weight. For example, a size 16 chicken weighs 1.6 kg. At a particular farm, the chickens they sell as size 15 have weights which are normally distributed with a mean of 1.56 kg and a standard deviation of 0.025 kg. Chickens that weigh less than 1.5 kg should be classified size 14 and chickens that weigh more than 1.6 kg should be classified size 16.

The following table gives the probability of scores with a $z$-score less than the given value.

\extable{504_q30_t1}

For example, the probability of a score with a $z$-score of less than 2.6 is 0.995, as highlighted above.

What is the probability that a randomly selected size 15 chicken has been incorrectly classified? Give your answer correct to the nearest 3 decimal places.

solutions.latex:
Convert the limits to $z$-scores using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$.

Chickens over $1.6$ kg:
$$z=\dfrac{1.6-1.56}{0.025}=1.6$$
Chickens under $1.5$ kg:
$$z=\dfrac{1.5-1.56}{0.025}=-2.4$$
The probability of incorrectly classifying a size 15 chicken is
$$\begin{aligned} 1-P(-2.4<z<1.6)&=P(z<-2.4)+P(z>1.6) \\ &=0.0082+0.0548 \\ &=0.063 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correctly determines the $z$-scores or one of the probabilities, or equivalent merit

5092.stem: Mimi borrows \$650 000 to buy a house at 6 % per annum with interest compounded monthly. The loan is to be repaid with equal monthly repayments of \$4200. Let $A_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ months.

parts.latex: After 15 years, the amount owing is \$373 722 to the nearest dollar. At this time Mimi borrows a further \$200 000 to build an extension. She adds this onto her previous mortgage. If the monthly repayments remain the same, what is the minimum remaining number of months it will take her to pay off the balance of the loan?

solutions.latex:
The amount owing grows by 0.5% per month ($6\%\div 12$) and falls by the repayment.
$$\begin{aligned} A_0&=650000 \\ A_1&=650000(1.005)-4200 \\ A_2&=\big(650000(1.005)-4200\big)\times 1.005-4200 \\ &=650000(1.005)^2-4200(1.005+1) \end{aligned}$$
Continuing this pattern,
$$A_n=650000(1.005)^n-4200\left(1.005^{n-1}+1.005^{n-2}+\ldots+1.005+1\right)$$
The bracket is a GP with $a=1$, $r=1.005$ and $n$ terms.
$$\begin{aligned} A_n&=650000(1.005)^n-4200\left(\dfrac{1.005^n-1}{1.005-1}\right) \\ &=650000(1.005)^n-840000\left(1.005^n-1\right) \\ &=840000-190000\times 1.005^n \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the sum of the GP, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress towards the solution

solutions.latex:
The new balance is $373722+200000=573722$.

Let $B_n$ be the amount owing after $n$ further months, so $B_0=573722$.
$$B_n=573722(1.005)^n-840000\left(1.005^n-1\right)$$
The loan is paid off when $B_n=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0&=573722(1.005)^n-840000\left(1.005^n-1\right) \\ (1.005)^n&=\dfrac{840000}{840000-573722} \\ n&=\dfrac{\ln\left(\frac{840000}{840000-573722}\right)}{\ln(1.005)} \\ &\approx 230.4 \text{ months} \end{aligned}$$
Since $n$ must be a whole number of months, round up.
$$\therefore\ \text{the loan is paid off after a further 231 months}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $(1.005)^n$, or equivalent merit
Determines the new balance, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Expand and simplify the expression $(x+4)(x-1)(x-3)$.

Consider the curves defined by the equations $y=\dfrac{12}{x}$ and $y=13-x^2$.

Using part (a), or otherwise, find the points of intersection between these two curves and find the exact area enclosed between the two curves in the first quadrant.

solutions.latex:
At intersections the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{12}{x}&=13-x^2 \\ 12&=13x-x^3 \\ x^3-13x+12&=0 \\ (x+4)(x-1)(x-3)&=0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=1,3,-4$, giving $y=12,4,-3$.

The points of intersection are $(1,12)$, $(3,4)$ and $(-4,-3)$.

In the first quadrant the curves enclose the region from $x=1$ to $x=3$, where $y=13-x^2$ is above $y=\dfrac{12}{x}$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=\int_1^3\left(13-x^2-\dfrac{12}{x}\right)dx \\ &=\left[13x-\dfrac{x^3}{3}-12\ln x\right]_1^3 \\ &=(39-9-12\ln 3)-\left(13-\dfrac{1}{3}-0\right) \\ &=17\dfrac{1}{3}-12\ln 3 \text{ units}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Correct area formula and integrates correctly, with correct bounds, or equivalent merit
Correct area formula and attempts to integrate correctly
Makes some progress towards the points of intersection
Makes some progress towards the answer

parts.latex: Solve $\log_3 x+\log_9 x=12$.

solutions.latex:
Applying the change of base rule, $\log_a b=\dfrac{\ln b}{\ln a}$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3}+\dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3^2}&=12 \\ \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln 3}+\dfrac{\ln x}{2\ln 3}&=12 \\ \dfrac{2\ln x+\ln x}{2\ln 3}&=12 \\ 3\ln x&=24\ln 3 \\ \ln x&=8\ln 3 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ x=3^8$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards the correct answer

parts.latex: Sophie rolls two dice and observes that the sum of the uppermost numbers is six. What is the probability that the number four has appeared at least once?

solutions.latex:
Let $E$ be the event that a 4 appears at least once, and $F$ the event that the sum is 6.
$$\begin{aligned} E&=\{(4,1),(4,2),(4,3),(4,4),(4,5),(4,6),(1,4),(2,4),(3,4),(5,4),(6,4)\} \\ F&=\{(1,5),(2,4),(3,3),(4,2),(5,1)\} \\ E\cap F&=\{(2,4),(4,2)\} \end{aligned}$$
So $P(E)=\dfrac{11}{36}$, $P(F)=\dfrac{5}{36}$ and $P(E\cap F)=\dfrac{2}{36}$.
$$\begin{aligned} P(E|F)&=\dfrac{P(E\cap F)}{P(F)} \\ &=\dfrac{\frac{2}{36}}{\frac{5}{36}} \\ &=\dfrac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Makes some progress towards the correct answer

parts.latex:
During the festival of lanterns Oscar releases a lantern from point $O$. It floats up into the sky due north in a straight line with an angle of elevation of $60^\circ$. Sarina is located at $S$, 10 metres from $O$ at a bearing of $\text{N}30^\circ\text{E}$ from $O$.

The lantern has travelled $3\sqrt{3}$ metres from $O$ when Sarina first observes it at $L$. The point $G$ is on the ground directly below $L$.

parts.note: 3D trigonometry (lantern at an elevation seen from a point on a bearing) is not in 2024 Advanced.

solutions.latex:
Let $LG=h$ and $\alpha=60^\circ$ be the angle of elevation.

In $\triangle OGL$, by Pythagoras' theorem,
$$OG=\sqrt{(3\sqrt{3})^2-h^2}$$
Also $OG=3\sqrt{3}\cos\alpha$.

In $\triangle SGL$, by Pythagoras' theorem,
$$SG=\sqrt{y^2-h^2}$$
In $\triangle OSG$, by the cosine rule:
$$\begin{aligned} SG^2&=OG^2+OS^2-2\times OG\times OS\times\cos 30^\circ \\ y^2-h^2&=(3\sqrt{3})^2-h^2+10^2-2\times 3\sqrt{3}\cos\alpha\times 10\times\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ y^2&=27+100-\dfrac{90}{2} \\ y&=\sqrt{82}\approx 9.055385\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ y\approx 9 \text{ m (to the nearest metre)}$$
criteria: Correct expression for $SG$ or $OG$, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress towards the correct answer

parts.latex: Two dangerous goods long-haul drivers are contracted to share the driving on one truckload of chemicals over a distance of 1200 km. They are each paid \$55 per hour for the time spent on the road. The truck consumes fuel at a rate of $10+\dfrac{v^2}{100}$ litres per hour where the average speed of the truck is $v$ km per hour. Diesel fuel costs \$1.50 per litre. Show that to complete the journey the cost $\$C$ of fuel and wages will be given by $C=\dfrac{150\,000}{v}+18v$, and determine the minimum cost. Give your answer correct to the nearest dollar.

solutions.latex:
Using $S=\dfrac{D}{T}$, the time taken is $T=\dfrac{1200}{v}$ hours.

Wages for two drivers:
$$55\times 2\times\dfrac{1200}{v}=\dfrac{132000}{v}$$
Fuel:
$$\left(10+\dfrac{v^2}{100}\right)\times\dfrac{1200}{v}\times 1.50=\left(10+\dfrac{v^2}{100}\right)\times\dfrac{1800}{v}=\dfrac{18000}{v}+18v$$
Total cost:
$$C=\dfrac{150000}{v}+18v$$
Differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dC}{dv}=-\dfrac{150000}{v^2}+18$$
Stationary points occur where $\dfrac{dC}{dv}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 18v^2&=150000 \\ v^2&=\dfrac{150000}{18} \\ v&\approx 91.287\ldots\approx 91 \text{ km/h} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2C}{dv^2}=\dfrac{300000}{v^3}$$
At $v=91$, $\dfrac{d^2C}{dv^2}=\dfrac{300000}{91^3}>0$, so this is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} C_{\min}&=\dfrac{150000}{91}+18\times 91 \\ &\approx 3286.35\ldots \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{minimum cost}\approx \$3286$$
criteria: Correctly determines the first and second derivatives, or equivalent merit
Makes some progress towards an expression for the cost
Makes some progress towards the correct answer

parts.latex: If $\cos\theta=-\dfrac{12}{13}$ and $180^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$, then $\cot\theta=$

solutions.latex:
Since $\cos\theta<0$ and $180^\circ\le\theta\le360^\circ$, $\theta$ is in the third quadrant, where $\tan\theta>0$.

Using the triangle with sides $5, 12, 13$:
$$\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}$$
$$\begin{aligned}\cot\theta&=\dfrac{1}{\tan\theta}\\&=\dfrac{12}{5}\end{aligned}$$
Hence the answer is option D.

parts.latex: What are the asymptotes of the graph of $y=\dfrac{1}{x^2-9}$

solutions.latex:
Vertical asymptotes occur where the denominator is zero.
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-9&=0\\(x-3)(x+3)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=\pm3$, which is option A.

parts.latex: For the function $f(x)=\dfrac{x^3}{3}-5x^2+2x+10$, the gradient is $-14$ at two points. What are the values of the $x$-coordinates at these points?

solutions.latex:
$$f'(x)=x^2-10x+2$$
Set the gradient equal to $-14$:
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-10x+2&=-14\\x^2-10x+16&=0\\(x-8)(x-2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=8, 2$, which is option B.

parts.latex: What is the domain of the function $f(x)=\sqrt{x}+\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2-x}}$?

solutions.latex:
$\sqrt{x}$ needs $x\ge0$.

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2-x}}$ needs $2-x>0$, so $x<2$.

Hence $0\le x<2$, that is $[0,\,2)$, which is option B.

parts.latex: If the $z$ scores on an examination are normally distributed and $P(z\le N)=0.6$ for some number $N$, what is the value of $P(-N\le z\le N)$?

solutions.latex:
By symmetry of the normal curve about $z=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}P(-N\le z\le N)&=2P(0\le z\le N)\\&=2\{P(z\le N)-0.5\}\\&=2(0.6-0.5)\\&=0.2\end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex: What is the change in amplitude and period when the function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x$ is transformed into $g(x)=\sin2x$?

solutions.latex:
For $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin4x$: amplitude $=\dfrac{1}{2}$, period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{4}=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.

For $g(x)=\sin2x$: amplitude $=1$, period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{2}=\pi$.

So the amplitude is doubled and the period is doubled, which is option D.

parts.latex: Which statement is true for an ungrouped data set with no outliers?
parts.note: IQR and outliers of a data set: removed from 2024 Advanced (Standard content)

solutions.latex:

parts.latex: Which line is perpendicular to $3x+4y+7=0$?

solutions.latex:
Rearrange $3x+4y+7=0$:
$$\begin{aligned}4y&=-3x-7\\y&=-\dfrac{3}{4}x-\dfrac{7}{4}\end{aligned}$$
So $m=-\dfrac{3}{4}$ and the perpendicular gradient is $m_\perp=\dfrac{4}{3}$.

Option C:
$$\begin{aligned}6y&=8x-7\\y&=\dfrac{4}{3}x-\dfrac{7}{6}\end{aligned}$$
The gradient is $\dfrac{4}{3}$, so the answer is option C.

parts.latex: What is the derivative of $3^{4x+5}$?

solutions.latex:
Using $\dfrac{d}{dx}a^{u}=\ln a\cdot u'\cdot a^{u}$ with $a=3$ and $u=4x+5$:
$$\dfrac{d}{dx}3^{4x+5}=\ln3\times4\times3^{4x+5}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex: What is the value of $\ln2+\ln4+\ln8+\dots+\ln2^{2n}$?

solutions.latex:
Using $\ln2^k=k\ln2$:
$$\begin{aligned}\ln2+\ln2^2+\dots+\ln2^{2n}&=\ln2+2\ln2+\dots+2n\ln2\\&=(1+2+3+\dots+2n)\ln2\end{aligned}$$
The bracket is an arithmetic series with $a=1$, $d=1$, $2n$ terms and last term $l=2n$:
$$\begin{aligned}S&=\dfrac{2n}{2}(1+2n)\\&=n(2n+1)\end{aligned}$$
So the sum is $n(2n+1)\ln2$, which is option D.

parts.latex:
Find the values of $a$ and $b$ (in simplified form) such that

$$\dfrac{3}{4-\sqrt{2}}=a+\sqrt{b}$$

solutions.latex:
Rationalise the denominator.
$$\begin{aligned}\dfrac{3}{4-\sqrt{2}}\times\dfrac{4+\sqrt{2}}{4+\sqrt{2}}&=\dfrac{12+3\sqrt{2}}{16-2}\\&=\dfrac{12+3\sqrt{2}}{14}\\&=\dfrac{6}{7}+\dfrac{3}{14}\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}$$
So $a=\dfrac{6}{7}$ and $\sqrt{b}=\dfrac{3}{14}\sqrt{2}$.
$$\begin{aligned}b&=\left(\dfrac{3\sqrt{2}}{14}\right)^2\\&=\dfrac{9\times2}{196}\\&=\dfrac{18}{196}\\&=\dfrac{9}{98}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=\dfrac{6}{7},\ b=\dfrac{9}{98}$$
criteria: Rationalises the denominator, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: What is the coordinate of $A$?
Find the area bounded by the $x$-axis and the curve $y=x^2-x-6$ for the interval $0\le x\le6$.

solutions.latex:
$A$ is an $x$-intercept, so set $y=0$.
$$\begin{aligned}x^2-x-6&=0\\(x-3)(x+2)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=3$ or $x=-2$. From the diagram $A$ is the positive intercept.
$$\therefore\ A(3,0)$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The curve is below the $x$-axis for $0\le x\le3$ and above it for $3\le x\le6$, so the two areas are found separately.
$$A=\displaystyle\int_3^6(x^2-x-6)\,dx+\left|\int_0^3(x^2-x-6)\,dx\right|$$
$$A=\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-6x\right]_3^6+\left|\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}-\dfrac{x^2}{2}-6x\right]_0^3\right|$$
$$A=\left(\dfrac{6^3}{3}-\dfrac{6^2}{2}-6(6)\right)-\left(\dfrac{3^3}{3}-\dfrac{3^2}{2}-6(3)\right)+\left|\left(\dfrac{3^3}{3}-\dfrac{3^2}{2}-6(3)\right)-0\right|$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=18+\dfrac{27}{2}+\dfrac{27}{2}\\&=45\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Sets up both integrals with correct antiderivative and limits, or equivalent merit
Finds the antiderivative, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the stationary points and determine their nature.
Show that a point of inflection occurs at $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

Sketch the graph $y=2x^3-9x^2+12x$, indicating clearly all important features.

solutions.latex:
Stationary points occur where $y'=0$.
$$y'=6x^2-18x+12$$
$$\begin{aligned}6x^2-18x+12&=0\\x^2-3x+2&=0\\(x-2)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=1$ or $x=2$. When $x=1$, $y=5$; when $x=2$, $y=4$.

The stationary points are $(1,5)$ and $(2,4)$.

Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$y''=12x-18$$
$$\begin{aligned}x=1:\ y''&=-6<0 &&\text{maximum}\\x=2:\ y''&=6>0 &&\text{minimum}\end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ (1,5)\text{ is a maximum and }(2,4)\text{ is a minimum}$$
criteria: Finds both stationary points, or equivalent merit
Finds $y'$ and sets it to zero, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
A point of inflection needs $y''=0$ and a change in concavity.
$$\begin{aligned}y''&=12x-18=0\\12x&=18\\x&=\dfrac{3}{2}\end{aligned}$$
Test the sign of $y''$ either side:
$$\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}x&1.25&1.5&1.75\\\hline y''&-3&0&3\end{array}$$
The concavity changes, so a point of inflection occurs at $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$.

parts.latex: Find the coordinates of the two points $P$ and $Q$ where the two curves intersect.
Hence, find in simplest form, the area of the shaded region contained between the two curves.

solutions.latex:
At an intersection the $y$ values are equal.
$$\begin{aligned}2-\dfrac{3}{x}&=x-2\\2x-3&=x^2-2x\\x^2-4x+3&=0\\(x-3)(x-1)&=0\end{aligned}$$
So $x=1$ or $x=3$.

When $x=1$, $y=-1$; when $x=3$, $y=1$.
$$\therefore\ P(1,-1)\text{ and }Q(3,1)$$
criteria: Finds both $x$ values, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The line is below the curve between $x=1$ and $x=3$, so the area is the integral of the curve minus the line.
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\displaystyle\int_1^3\left[2-\dfrac{3}{x}-(x-2)\right]dx\\&=\int_1^3\left(4-\dfrac{3}{x}-x\right)dx\\&=\left[4x-3\ln x-\dfrac{x^2}{2}\right]_1^3\end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned}A&=\left(4(3)-3\ln3-\dfrac{3^2}{2}\right)-\left(4-3\ln1-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)\\&=12-3\ln3-\dfrac{9}{2}-4+\dfrac{1}{2}\\&=(4-3\ln3)\text{ units}^2\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the correct antiderivative, or equivalent merit

Solve the equation $\log_2x=4\log_x2$

$$\begin{aligned}\log_x2&=\dfrac{\log_22}{\log_2x}\\&=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}\end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Using part (a), $\log_x2=\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}$:
$$\begin{aligned}\log_2x&=4\times\dfrac{1}{\log_2x}\\(\log_2x)^2&=4\\\log_2x&=\pm2\end{aligned}$$
If $\log_2x=2$, then $x=2^2=4$.

If $\log_2x=-2$, then $x=2^{-2}=\dfrac{1}{4}$.
$$\therefore\ x=4\text{ or }x=\dfrac{1}{4}$$

parts.latex: The completion times for the Oztown triathlon race were normally distributed with mean times 60 minutes and standard deviation 5 minutes. Using the empirical rule, find Ozzie's completion time if he finished ahead of $84\%$ of competitors.

solutions.latex:
By the empirical rule, $68\%$ of values lie within one standard deviation of the mean, so $34\%$ lie between $\mu-\sigma$ and $\mu$.
$$50\%+\dfrac{1}{2}\times68\%=84\%$$
So $84\%$ of times are greater than $\mu-\sigma$. Finishing ahead of $84\%$ of competitors means a time one standard deviation below the mean.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{Time}&=60-5\\&=55\text{ minutes}\end{aligned}$$
criteria: Identifies that the time is one standard deviation from the mean, or equivalent merit

Show that the two equations in terms of $a$ and $b$ are

$$a+b=0.25$$

solutions.latex:
The probabilities sum to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+0.45+a+b&=1 \\ 0.75+a+b&=1 \end{aligned}$$
So $a+b=0.25$.

The mean is 2, so $\sum xP(x)=2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 0.3+2(0.45)+3a+4b&=2 \\ 0.3+0.9+3a+4b&=2 \\ 1.2+3a+4b&=2 \end{aligned}$$
So $3a+4b=0.8$.
criteria: Obtains one of the equations, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Multiply $a+b=0.25$ by 4.
$$4a+4b=1 \quad \cdots (1)$$
$$3a+4b=0.8 \quad \cdots (2)$$
Subtracting $(2)$ from $(1)$ gives $a=0.2$.

Substitute into $(1)$.
$$\begin{aligned} 4(0.2)+4b&=1 \\ 0.8+4b&=1 \\ 4b&=0.2 \\ b&=0.05 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ a=0.2,\ b=0.05$$
criteria: Finds one of $a$ or $b$, or equivalent merit

Hence find the minimum area of metal required.

solutions.latex:
The volume of a prism is $V=Ah$, where the base area is $2x\cdot x=2x^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 9&=2x^2h \\ h&=\dfrac{9}{2x^2} \quad \cdots (1) \end{aligned}$$
The surface area is two bases, two sides of $2x$ by $h$ and two ends of $x$ by $h$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=2(2x^2)+2(2xh)+2(xh) \\ &=4x^2+4xh+2xh \\ &=4x^2+6xh \quad \cdots (2) \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $(1)$ into $(2)$.
$$\begin{aligned} A&=4x^2+6x\left(\dfrac{9}{2x^2}\right) \\ &=4x^2+\dfrac{27}{x} \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $h$ in terms of $x$ or the surface area in terms of $x$ and $h$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Write $A=4x^2+27x^{-1}$ and differentiate.
$$\dfrac{dA}{dx}=8x-27x^{-2}=8x-\dfrac{27}{x^2}$$
Stationary points occur when $\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 8x-\dfrac{27}{x^2}&=0 \\ 8x^3-27&=0 \\ x^3&=\dfrac{27}{8} \\ x&=\dfrac{3}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Test the nature using the second derivative.
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=8+54x^{-3}=8+\dfrac{54}{x^3}$$
When $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$:
$$\dfrac{d^2A}{dx^2}=8+\dfrac{54}{\left(\frac{3}{2}\right)^3}=24>0$$
so it is a minimum.
$$\begin{aligned} A_{\min}&=4\left(\dfrac{3}{2}\right)^2+\dfrac{27}{\frac{3}{2}} \\ &=9+18 \\ &=27 \text{ m}^2 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds $x=\dfrac{3}{2}$ and shows it gives a minimum, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: At time ($t$ hours) after 12:00 am, the height ($h$ metres) of the deck of a boat above the level of the jetty is given by $h=2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+1$. Find, correct to the nearest minute, the first time after 12:00 am when the deck of the boat is level with the jetty.

solutions.latex:
The deck is level with the jetty when $h=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2\cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)+1&=0 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t\right)&=-\dfrac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$$
Cosine is negative in the second and third quadrants.
$$\dfrac{4\pi}{25}t=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},\ \dfrac{4\pi}{3},\ \dots$$
So $t=\dfrac{25}{6},\ \dfrac{25}{3},\ \dots$

The first time is $t=\dfrac{25}{6}$ hours, which is 4:10 am.

parts.latex: If $y=\tan^2x$, find the values of the constants $a$ and $b$, such that $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=ay^2+by+2$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiate using the chain rule, then write in terms of $\tan x$ using $\sec^2x=1+\tan^2x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx}&=2\tan x\sec^2x \\ &=2\tan x(1+\tan^2x) \\ &=2\tan x+2\tan^3x \end{aligned}$$
Differentiate again.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}&=2\sec^2x+6\tan^2x\sec^2x \\ &=2(1+\tan^2x)+6\tan^2x(1+\tan^2x) \\ &=2+2\tan^2x+6\tan^2x+6\tan^4x \\ &=2+8\tan^2x+6\tan^4x \end{aligned}$$
Substitute $y=\tan^2x$.
$$\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}=6y^2+8y+2$$
$$\therefore\ a=6,\ b=8$$
criteria: Finds $\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ in terms of $\tan x$, or equivalent merit

5133.stem: The continuous random variable $X$ has probability density function $f(x)=\dfrac{1}{2}\sin x$ for $0\le x\le\pi$.

parts.latex: Find the cumulative distributive function (CDF)
Find the first quartile of the distribution.

solutions.latex:
The CDF is $F(x)=\displaystyle\int_0^x f(t)\,dt$.
$$\begin{aligned} F(x)&=\int_0^x\dfrac{1}{2}\sin t\,dt \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}\left[\cos t\right]_0^x \\ &=-\dfrac{1}{2}(\cos x-1) \\ &=\dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the primitive, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
The first quartile satisfies $F(x)=0.25$.
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{1}{2}(1-\cos x)&=\dfrac{1}{4} \\ 1-\cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ \cos x&=\dfrac{1}{2} \\ x&=\dfrac{\pi}{3} \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Differentiate $x\log_ex$.

solutions.latex:
Using the product rule, $\dfrac{d}{dx}(uv)=u'v+uv'$, with
$$\begin{aligned} u&=x & v&=\log_ex \\ u'&=1 & v'&=\dfrac{1}{x} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_ex)&=x\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)+\log_ex(1) \\ &=1+\log_ex \end{aligned}$$
So $\log_ex=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_ex)-1$.

solutions.latex:
Using $\log_ex=\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\log_ex)-1$ from part (a), a primitive of $\log_ex$ is $x\log_ex-x$.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_1^2\log_ex\,dx&=\left[x\log_ex-x\right]_1^2 \\ &=2\log_e2-2-(\log_e1-1) \\ &=2\log_e2-2+1 \\ &=2\log_e2-1 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the primitive, or equivalent merit

5135.stem: At time $t$ years after it was purchased the value $\$V$ of a car is given by $V=25\,000e^{-0.5t}$.

parts.latex: Find the loss in value of the car during the third year.
Find the year in which the car is losing value at a rate of $\$100$ per year.

solutions.latex:
$$V=25\,000e^{-0.5t}$$
$$\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-12\,500e^{-0.5t}$$
The third year runs from $t=2$ to $t=3$, so the loss is $V(2)-V(3)$:
$$\begin{aligned} V(2)-V(3)&=25\,000e^{-1}-25\,000e^{-1.5} \\ &=25\,000\left(e^{-1}-e^{-1.5}\right) \\ &\approx\$3618.73 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the car loses about }\$3618.73\text{ in the third year}$$

solutions.latex:
The rate of loss is $100$ per year, so $\dfrac{dV}{dt}=-100$.
$$\begin{aligned} -12\,500e^{-0.5t}&=-100 \\ e^{-0.5t}&=\dfrac{1}{125} \\ -0.5t&=\ln\left(\dfrac{1}{125}\right) \\ -0.5t&=-\ln125 \\ t&=\dfrac{\ln125}{0.5} \\ &\approx 9.6566 \end{aligned}$$
So the car is losing value at $\$100$ per year during the 10th year.
criteria: Forms and solves $e^{-0.5t}=\dfrac{1}{125}$ for $t$, or equivalent merit

5137.stem: A particle is moving in a straight line. At time $t$ seconds it has a displacement $x$ metres from a fixed point $O$ on the line, velocity $v$ ms$^{-1}$, and acceleration $a$ ms$^{-2}$ is given by $a=6t-12$. Initially, the particle is at rest at $O$.

parts.latex: Find expressions for $v$ and $x$ in terms of $t$.
Find when and where the particle is next at rest.

solutions.latex:
Integrate the acceleration.
$$v=\dfrac{6t^2}{2}-12t+c=3t^2-12t+c$$
When $t=0$, $v=0$, so $c=0$ and $v=3t^2-12t$.

Integrate the velocity.
$$x=\dfrac{3t^3}{3}-\dfrac{12t^2}{2}+c=t^3-6t^2+c$$
When $t=0$, $x=0$, so $c=0$.
$$\therefore\ v=3t^2-12t,\quad x=t^3-6t^2$$
criteria: Finds $v$ and integrates to find $x$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
The particle is at rest when $v=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} 3t^2-12t&=0 \\ 3t(t-4)&=0 \\ t&=0,\ 4 \end{aligned}$$
The particle is next at rest at $t=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} x&=4^3-6(4)^2 \\ &=-32 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the particle is next at rest when } t=4 \text{ s, 32 m to the left of the origin}$$

figures.cap: graph of y = (e^x - e^-x)/(e^x + e^-x) with asymptotes y = 1, y = -1 and shaded region up to x = k

parts.latex: Show that the shaded region bounded by the curve, the $x$ axis and the line $x=k$, where $k>0$, has area $\ln\left(\dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}\right)$.
Find, in simplest exact form, the value of $k$ such that the shaded region has area of 1 square unit.

solutions.latex:
The area is $\displaystyle\int_0^k y\,dx$. The numerator is the derivative of the denominator, so the primitive is a logarithm.
$$\begin{aligned} \int_0^k\dfrac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}\,dx&=\left[\ln(e^x+e^{-x})\right]_0^k \\ &=\ln(e^k+e^{-k})-\ln(e^0+e^0) \\ &=\ln(e^k+e^{-k})-\ln2 \\ &=\ln\left(\dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}\right) \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Finds the primitive, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
Set the area equal to 1.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln\left(\dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}\right)&=1 \\ \dfrac{e^k+e^{-k}}{2}&=e \\ e^k+e^{-k}&=2e \end{aligned}$$
Multiply each term by $e^k$.
$$(e^k)^2+1=2e(e^k)$$
$$(e^k)^2-2e(e^k)+1=0$$
Let $m=e^k$, so $m^2-2em+1=0$.
$$\begin{aligned} m&=\dfrac{2e\pm\sqrt{(-2e)^2-4(1)(1)}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{2e\pm\sqrt{4e^2-4}}{2} \\ &=\dfrac{2e\pm2\sqrt{e^2-1}}{2} \\ &=e\pm\sqrt{e^2-1} \end{aligned}$$
Since $m=e^k$:
Since $k>0$, $e^k>1$, and $e-\sqrt{e^2-1}\approx0.19<1$ is rejected.
$$\therefore\ k=\ln\left(e+\sqrt{e^2-1}\right)\ (\approx1.657)$$
criteria: Forms the quadratic in $e^k$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: If $a, b$ and $c$ are positive numbers, and $\ln 3a = \ln b - 2\ln c$, which of the following is true?

solutions.latex:
Using the log laws, $\ln b - 2\ln c = \ln b - \ln c^2$.
$$\begin{aligned} \ln 3a &= \ln\dfrac{b}{c^2} \\ 3a &= \dfrac{b}{c^2} \\ a &= \dfrac{b}{3c^2} \end{aligned}$$
This matches option B.

parts.latex: The difference in volume between two sources of sound $P_1$ and $P_2$ is defined to be $10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right)$ decibels. How much louder is a sound of 112 dB than a sound of 80 dB?

solutions.latex:
The difference in volume is $112 - 80 = 32$ dB.
$$\begin{aligned} 10\log_{10}\left(\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right) &= 32 \\ \log_{10}\left(\dfrac{P_1}{P_2}\right) &= 3.2 \\ \dfrac{P_1}{P_2} &= 10^{3.2} \\ P_1 &\approx 1585P_2 \end{aligned}$$
The 112 dB sound is about 1585 times louder, which is option B.

parts.latex:
The population ($N$) of a town after $t$ years, is given by the formula $N = Ae^{0.04t}$, where $A$ is the initial population.

Which expression represents the number of years it takes until the town has doubled its population?

solutions.latex:
Doubling means $N = 2A$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2A &= Ae^{0.04t} \\ e^{0.04t} &= 2 \\ 0.04t &= \ln 2 \\ t &= \dfrac{\ln 2}{0.04} \\ &= \dfrac{100\ln 2}{4} \\ &= 25\log_e 2 \end{aligned}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: Given $\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}$ and $\sin\theta > 0$, find $\cot\theta$.

solutions.latex:
Since $\cos\theta = \dfrac{12}{13}$ and $\sin\theta>0$, use a right-angled triangle with adjacent $12$ and hypotenuse $13$.

By Pythagoras' theorem, the opposite side is $\sqrt{13^2-12^2}=5$.
$$\cot\theta = \dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{opposite}} = \dfrac{12}{5}$$
This matches option D.

parts.latex: Show that $\log_x 5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x}$
Hence, or otherwise, solve the equation $\log_5 x = 4\log_x 5$

solutions.latex:
Using the change of base formula to base 5:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_x 5 &= \dfrac{\log_5 5}{\log_5 x} \\ &= \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x} \text{ since } \log_5 5 = 1 \end{aligned}$$

From part (a), $\log_x 5 = \dfrac{1}{\log_5 x}$, so the equation becomes
$$\begin{aligned} \log_5 x &= \dfrac{4}{\log_5 x} \\ (\log_5 x)^2 &= 4 \\ \log_5 x &= \pm 2 \end{aligned}$$
If $\log_5 x = 2$, then $x = 5^2 = 25$.

If $\log_5 x = -2$, then $x = 5^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{25}$.
$$\therefore\ x = 25 \text{ or } x = \dfrac{1}{25}$$

parts.latex: Show that the gradient of the tangent to the curve $y = 3e^{-x}$ at $x = -1$ is $m = -3e$.
Hence, or otherwise, find the equation of the normal to the curve $y = 3e^{-x}$ at $x = -1$.

solutions.latex:
Differentiating $y = 3e^{-x}$:
$$\dfrac{dy}{dx} = -3e^{-x}$$
At $x=-1$:
$$\begin{aligned} \dfrac{dy}{dx} &= -3e^{-(-1)} \\ &= -3e \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ m = -3e$$

solutions.latex:

At $x=-1$:

The normal passes through $(-1, 3e)$:
$$\begin{aligned} y - 3e &= \dfrac{1}{3e}(x+1) \\ 3e(y-3e) &= x+1 \\ x - 3ey + 9e^2 + 1 &= 0 \end{aligned}$$

parts.latex: Solve the equation $\log_2(x-3) + \log_2(x+4) = 3,\ x > 3$

solutions.latex:
Using the log law for addition:
$$\begin{aligned} \log_2(x-3)(x+4) &= 3 \\ \log_2(x^2+x-12) &= 3 \\ x^2+x-12 &= 2^3 \\ x^2+x-20 &= 0 \\ (x-4)(x+5) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $x=4$ or $x=-5$.

Since $x>3$, reject $x=-5$.
$$\therefore\ x = 4$$

parts.latex:
Solve $3\sin\theta - 2\operatorname{cosec}\theta = 5$ for $0 \le \theta \le 2\pi$.

Give your answer(s) to 3 significant figures.

solutions.latex:
Using $\operatorname{cosec}\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$:
$$\begin{aligned} 3\sin\theta - \dfrac{2}{\sin\theta} &= 5 \\ 3\sin^2\theta - 2 - 5\sin\theta &= 0 \\ (3\sin\theta + 1)(\sin\theta - 2) &= 0 \end{aligned}$$
So $\sin\theta = -\dfrac{1}{3}$ or $\sin\theta = 2$.

$\sin\theta = 2$ has no solutions as $-1 \le \sin\theta \le 1$.

5154.stem:
In Cherry Harbour, the height of the water above sea level, $h$ (in metres), is modelled by the function $h = 6.5 - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)$ where $t$ is the number of hours after midnight on Saturday.

Boats can safely enter the Harbour when the water is at least 7 metres above sea level.

figures.cap: solution sketch: hand-drawn graph of h against t over 24 hours

parts.latex: By considering the transformation of $h = \cos t$, draw a graph showing the height of the water in the harbour for the 24 hours commencing at midnight on Saturday.
Show that the earliest time for a boat to enter Cherry Harbour on Sunday is 6.58am.
How long can boats enter Cherry Harbour before the water is too shallow again? Give your answer to the nearest minute.

solutions.latex:
The graph of $h = 6.5 - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right)$ has period $\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/12} = 24$.

\exfigure{630_q16_s1}
criteria: Labels the axes and shows some steps towards the graph, or equivalent merit
Draws the initial graph, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Boats can enter when $h=7$:
$$\begin{aligned} 7 &= 6.5 - 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right) \\ 2\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right) &= -0.5 \\ \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{12}t\right) &= -0.25 \end{aligned}$$
The reference angle is $1.318$. For the first time after midnight, $\dfrac{\pi}{12}t = \pi - 1.318$.
$$\begin{aligned} t &= \dfrac{\pi - 1.318}{\frac{\pi}{12}} \\ &\approx 6.9656 \\ &\approx 6 \text{ h } 58 \text{ min} \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{the earliest time is } 6.58 \text{ am}$$
criteria: Makes some progress, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Source computes $0.9656$ h as 58 min and writes 6.58 am; kept.

solutions.latex:
Boats can enter when $h \ge 7$, that is when
$$\pi - 1.318 \le \dfrac{\pi}{12}t \le \pi + 1.318$$
Multiplying by $\dfrac{12}{\pi}$:
$$\dfrac{12(\pi - 1.318)}{\pi} \le t \le \dfrac{12(\pi + 1.318)}{\pi}$$
That is, $6.58$ am $\le t \le 5.02$ pm.
$$\therefore\ \text{boats can enter for } 10 \text{ h } 4 \text{ min, between } 6.58 \text{ am and } 5.02 \text{ pm}$$
criteria: Makes some progress, or equivalent merit
